questions.question: Git merge vs rebase vs squash — which integration strategy and why?
questions.title: Git Merge vs Rebase vs Squash: Integration Strategy Compared
questions.direct_answer: Use **merge** for shared/long-lived branches where preserving history matters — default for `develop`/`main` integration in GitFlow. Use **rebase** for keeping your feature branch's history linear before opening a PR — cleaner review, no merge bubbles. Use **squash-and-merge** for landing PRs into main — main has one commit per feature, easy revert, clean history. The rule: rebase locally, squash when landing, never rebase shared branches.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical Git workflow understanding and history hygiene
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Rebasing a branch that someone else has based their work on — they get a divergent history that's painful to reconcile
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss the 'rebase locally, merge publicly' rule, semantic commits in main, the bisect implications of squash-and-merge, and merge-queue (graphite/aviator) as the modern evolution

sections.title: Three Strategies, Three Different History Shapes
sections.content:
Git's three integration strategies produce different histories with different trade-offs:

**Merge commit (`git merge`)** creates an explicit merge commit that joins two branches. The branch history is preserved in full — every commit on the feature branch remains, plus a new merge commit ties them back to main. Result: a non-linear history with branches and merge bubbles. Useful when the branch's commit history tells a meaningful story (e.g., a long-lived release branch) or when you need full traceability.

**Rebase (`git rebase main`)** replays your branch commits one at a time on top of the latest main. Result: a linear history with no merge commits — it looks like you did your work directly on main. Cleaner to read, easier to bisect, but rewrites commit hashes (so don't rebase shared branches).

**Squash-and-merge** combines all branch commits into one new commit on main. Result: main has one commit per feature, no branch noise. Trade-off: lose granular history of how the feature evolved. Best when feature branches have many WIP/cleanup commits that don't add value to long-term history.

The most common modern pattern combines these: rebase your feature branch on main before review (clean history), squash-and-merge when landing (one commit per feature in main).

sections.title: How Each Strategy Shapes the Commit Graph
sections.content:
```mermaid
gitGraph
    commit id: "A"
    commit id: "B"
    branch feature
    commit id: "f1"
    commit id: "f2"
    commit id: "f3"
    checkout main
    commit id: "C"
    merge feature id: "merge commit"
    commit id: "D"
```

**Merge commit (above)**: feature branch commits f1, f2, f3 are preserved; the explicit merge commit shows where the branch joined main; history is non-linear with a branch bubble.

**Rebase**: replays f1, f2, f3 on top of C; no merge commit; main's history shows A, B, C, f1', f2', f3' (note primed hashes — commits are recreated).

**Squash-and-merge**: collapses f1, f2, f3 into one new commit on main; main shows A, B, C, [feature], D — one commit per feature; no branch history retained.

The shape of the graph determines how easy your history is to navigate, bisect, and revert.

sections.title: Strategy Comparison
sections.content:
| Aspect | Merge | Rebase | Squash-and-merge |
|--------|-------|--------|------------------|
| **Resulting history** | Non-linear, branch bubbles | Linear | Linear, one commit per feature |
| **Preserves branch commits** | Yes (all) | Yes (rewritten hashes) | No (collapsed into one) |
| **Bisect friendliness** | Medium (must skip merge commits) | Excellent | Excellent (one commit per change) |
| **Revert friendliness** | Hard (must revert merge commit + handle parent) | Per commit | Easy (revert one commit per feature) |
| **Safe on shared branches** | Yes | NO — rewrites history | Squash on main is safe; shared squash-only on PR's branch |
| **Common in** | GitFlow, traditional enterprise | Trunk-based, modern teams | GitHub PR default, modern SaaS teams |
| **Use case** | Long-lived branches, full audit | Cleaning local history before PR | Landing PRs into main |
| **Loses commit granularity** | No | No | Yes (intentional) |
| **Risk** | Branchy history, merge conflicts on long branches | Force-push on shared branch confuses team | Lose detail of how feature evolved |

sections.title: The Modern Recommended Workflow
sections.content:
**Step 1 — Rebase locally before opening a PR.**

```bash
git checkout feature/payment-flow
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main
# resolve any conflicts
git push --force-with-lease
```

This keeps your branch on top of latest main, so the diff in the PR is clean and there's no merge bubble. `--force-with-lease` is safer than `--force` — it refuses to overwrite if someone else pushed to your branch.

**Step 2 — Interactive rebase to clean up commits.**

```bash
git rebase -i origin/main
# in editor: pick / squash / fixup / reword
```

Combine WIP commits, fix typos in commit messages, reorder for logical flow. Each commit on your branch should be a meaningful unit (a refactor, a feature, a test add).

**Step 3 — Open PR; reviewer reviews the clean history.**

Good commits make review easier — each commit is a logical step the reviewer can follow.

**Step 4 — Squash-and-merge into main.**

GitHub's "Squash and merge" button collapses your PR commits into one new commit on main with the PR title as the message. Main stays clean: one commit per feature.

Result: main has linear, atomic history (one commit per merged PR); each commit is easily revertible; bisect is straightforward; the PR retains the granular history for audit.

**The forbidden actions:**
- **Never `git rebase` a branch others have based work on.** Their commits will be on a stale base after your rebase, and reconciling is painful.
- **Never `git push --force` to main or shared branches.** Use `--force-with-lease` only on your own feature branches.
- **Avoid `git pull` (which does merge by default).** Configure `pull.rebase = true` so `git pull` rebases instead of creating a merge commit on every sync.

sections.title: Trade-offs and Subtle Pitfalls
sections.content:
**Squash-and-merge loses bisect granularity within a feature.** If a PR squashes 20 commits, and one of those introduced a subtle bug, bisect points you at the squashed commit — you've lost the ability to bisect the 20 sub-commits. Mitigation: keep PRs small (one logical change per PR); for bug-prone areas, prefer per-commit merging.

**Merge commits in main make bisect noisy.** `git bisect` skips merge commits by default but the history is harder to read. Squash-and-merge produces the cleanest bisect experience.

**Rebase changes commit hashes.** A commit's identity changes after rebase. Anyone who pulled the pre-rebase branch sees divergent history when they fetch. The discipline: only rebase branches you alone work on, and communicate before force-pushing.

**Long-lived branches accumulate merge conflicts.** A feature branch open for 2 weeks accumulates conflicts with main. Rebasing weekly (or daily) keeps conflicts small. The longer you wait, the bigger the rebase pain.

**Merge queues (Graphite, Aviator, GitHub merge queue) are the modern evolution.** They serialize merges into main to prevent the "green PR breaks main on merge" race condition: PR A passes CI on commit X, PR B passes CI on commit X, both merge — result on main may not pass CI. Merge queues rebase-and-test each PR before letting it land. Worth adopting for high-volume repos.

**Semantic commit messages matter for squash-and-merge.** Since main has one commit per PR, the squash commit message becomes the long-lived history. Use Conventional Commits (`feat:`, `fix:`, `refactor:`) and meaningful descriptions — not the default GitHub squash title that includes the PR number.

**The rebase-vs-merge debate is a religion.** Consistent practice within a team matters more than the specific choice. Pick a convention; document it; enforce via tooling.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Merge** preserves full branch history with explicit merge commits — best for long-lived shared branches; produces non-linear history
- **Rebase** replays commits linearly on top of main — cleanest history, easy bisect; rewrites commit hashes so never use on shared branches
- **Squash-and-merge** collapses PR commits into one main commit — cleanest main history, easy revert; loses sub-commit bisect granularity
- **Modern workflow**: rebase locally to clean your branch, squash-and-merge when landing PRs into main
- **Never rebase shared branches**: `git rebase` rewrites history; pulling collaborators lose their work; use `--force-with-lease` (not `--force`) on personal branches only
- **Merge queues** (Graphite, Aviator, GitHub) are the modern evolution — prevent green-PR-breaks-main race conditions in high-volume repos

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Three Git integration strategies that produce three different history shapes. The right choice depends on what you value: full history preservation, linear readability, or atomic main commits.

**Merge commit — preserves branch history**
- Creates an explicit merge commit joining the branches; all feature commits remain visible; main history becomes non-linear with branch bubbles
- Best for long-lived shared branches where the full commit history tells a meaningful story; typical in GitFlow integrating release branches

**Rebase — linear local history**
- Replays your branch commits one at a time on top of latest main; no merge commit; result looks like you did the work directly on main
- Cleanest to read, easiest to bisect; the catch: rewrites commit hashes, so never rebase a branch someone else has based work on
- Use locally to keep your feature branch on top of main before opening or updating a PR

**Squash-and-merge — one commit per feature in main**
- Collapses all PR commits into one new commit on main; the squashed commit message becomes the long-lived history
- Cleanest main history, easy to revert one feature, but loses sub-commit granularity for bisect within a single PR
- The modern default for landing PRs in trunk-based and GitHub-flow teams

**The recommended modern workflow**
- Rebase locally to clean your branch's history before review; interactive rebase to combine WIP commits, fix messages, reorder for logical flow
- Use `git push --force-with-lease` — safer than `--force`, refuses to overwrite if someone pushed to your branch
- Open the PR with clean history; reviewer can follow each commit as a logical step
- Squash-and-merge into main; main has linear, atomic history; one commit per merged feature; easily revertible

**Trade-offs to call out**
- Squash-and-merge loses bisect granularity within a feature — mitigation is keeping PRs small, one logical change per PR
- Merge commits make bisect noisier; squash produces the cleanest bisect experience
- Long-lived branches accumulate merge conflicts; rebase weekly to keep conflicts small; the longer you wait, the worse the rebase

**The forbidden actions**
- Never rebase a branch others have based their work on; their commits land on a stale base and reconciling is painful
- Never force-push to main or shared branches; use `--force-with-lease` only on your own feature branches
- Avoid `git pull` defaulting to merge; configure `pull.rebase = true` so `git pull` rebases instead of creating a merge commit on every sync

**The modern evolution**
- Merge queues like Graphite, Aviator, and GitHub's built-in merge queue serialize merges into main; they prevent the race condition where two PRs each pass CI but the combined result on main breaks
- Worth adopting in high-volume repos where multiple PRs land per hour

**Cultural note**
- The rebase-vs-merge debate is religious; what matters more than the specific choice is consistent practice within a team; pick a convention, document it, enforce via tooling like branch protection and squash-only merges
